newsitem.title: USA: Two Latam countries post deflation in August.
newsitem.headline: Two Latam countries post deflation in August.

text.p: Argentina and Nicaragua posted negative inflation in August while Mexico had the lowest price increases since its 1994 devaluation, official figures showed.

In its fourth monthly deflation since January, Argentina showed a 0.10 percent decrease in consumer prices for an accumulated fall of 0.30 percent in the first eight months of 1996 -- by far the lowest figure in Latin America.

But these results stem not only from the success of a stabilisation plan, but also from an economic stagnation that nine out of 10 Argentines do not think will be overcome in the short-term, according to a poll published this week.
The decline in Nicaraguan prices was even steeper, with a 0.70 percent fall led by food and clothing sectors.
Another state that might soon join the countries with price declines is Brazil, which two years ago was struggling to escape from hyperinflation.

Brazil posted a 0.50 percent increase in the National Consumer Price Index, but the Getulio Vargas Foundation's IGP-M index fell by 0.40 percent in the last 10 days of August and might herald an overall fall in September.
Analysts agree however that falling prices are not a sign of things to come.
"This number was really surprising, but the index is very volatile. It does not mean we will be in a period of deflation", said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Brazil.
Mexico also had good news as inflation fell to 1.33 percent, the lowest level since the financial crisis that erupted in December 1994.
The impact of the peso devaluation, which sent prices spiralling, is still felt on a 18.50 percent accumulated rise for the January-August period, the second highest in Latin America.
The top place, far from any other country in the region, was for Venezuela, with a 4.1 percent rise in consumer prices in August that pushed the eight-month number to 70.4 percent.
